newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland peace hopes dim with explosives find.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland peace hopes dim with explosives find.

text.p: Hopes of a truce by IRA guerrillas were dimmer on Monday after police in Northern Ireland found a large quantity of home-made explosives they said was one step away from being turned into a bomb.
Fresh violence hit the province overnight when security force officers in the cities of Belfast and Londonderry were attacked by youths throwing stones and petrol bombs, police said.
Britain's Press Association news agency quoted a police spokesman as saying a soldier and two police officers suffered minor injuries in an attack in west Belfast.

Around 300 lb (150 kg) of the home-made explosives, a favoured weapon of Irish Republican Army guerrillas fighting British rule in Northern Ireland, was found on Sunday in three plastic bins in a coal shed at the back of a house in Londonderry, a heavily Catholic and Irish nationalist city.
Another two bags of explosives were found as police evacuated 50 houses and searched the area into the night.
"It was just one step away from being fully functional," said a police spokesman. "It was meant to be planted and it was meant to cause death."

Police said they had no idea about the likely target of the bomb and declined to comment on who they believed had hidden the explosives, although they said the location of the find pointed to republican guerrillas.

The discovery was announced just hours after Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein, appeared to dash hopes of a new IRA ceasefire which would pave the way for his party's admission to Northern Ireland peace talks.

As the province tried to recover from a week of violence sparked by parades by pro-British Protestant groups, Adams said demands that the guerrillas should start handing in their weapons remained a stumbling block.
Adams, responding to Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, said in a statement that the surrender of arms held by his guerrilla allies "still remains a major difficulty".

Mowlam had appealed earlier on Sunday for a new ceasefire by the IRA, a move which would win Sinn Fein a seat at peace talks within six weeks, saying: "Let the IRA/Sinn Fein make their decision, the ball is in their court."
But Protestant Unionists loyal to British rule dismissed hopes of a new IRA truce as "wishful thinking".

"The reality is that Sinn Fein/IRA are committed to violence in order to achieve objectives that no democrat can support," said David Trimble, the head of Northern Ireland's biggest pro-British group, the Ulster Unionist party.
Hopes of progress towards peace had risen after the Protestant Orange Order scrapped four parades over the weekend that had been routed through Catholic areas and were likely to spark rioting.

The marches, on a day when the Orange Order recalls a 1690 Protestant victory over a Catholic king, were cancelled after the threat of mass counter-demonstrations by Catholics who see the parades as intimidation.
A Protestant march along the Catholic Garvaghy Road in Portadown a week ago sparked some of the worst violence seen in the province in recent years.

Hundreds of other marches went ahead on Saturday, but moderate Catholic nationalist leader John Hume hailed the "moral courage" of the Orange Order for calling off the four flashpoint parades and defusing fears of sectarian strife.

Tension was high again however after the explosives find and Adams's statement, which echoed the IRA position that the scrapping of weapons should take place at the end of talks on a settlement between the Unionists and pro-Irish nationalists.
Britain's new Labour government has dropped demands for the IRA to disarm before Sinn Fein can join the talks, but is still insisting the guerrillas must give up weapons during the talks.
